title: Bellarmine: acquisition, increase, and forensic declaration
source_text: XVIII. Similia docet Bellarminus de Justif. lib. 1. cap. 3. inter alia enim observat nomen justificationis in sacris litteris accipi pro acquisitione justitiae, ut 1. Cor. 6. Haec quidem fuistis, sed abluti estis, sed sanctificati estis, sed justificati estis. Ad Rom. 8. Quos vocavit hos justificavit. Deinde, pro incremento justitiae. Nam, inquit, quemadmodum aestate dicitur calefieri, non solum qui fit calidus ex frigido, sed etiam qui ex calido fit calidior; sic etiam justificari dicitur, non solum is qui ex impio fit justus, sed ille quoque qui ex justo fit justior. Sic loquitur Ecclesiasticus, cap. 18. Ne verearis usque ad mortem justificari; & Jacobus in Epistola sua, cap. 2. Videtis quod ex operibus justificatur homo, & non ex fide tantum: & Joannes in Apoc. cap. 22. Qui justus est, justificetur adhuc. Denique, pro declaratione justitiae, modo quodam forensi, ut ille dicatur justificari, qui cum esset absens, aut etiam reus alicujus iniquitatis, a judice per sententiam declaratur justus, atque absolvitur. Sic utitur hac voce Salomon, Proverb. 17. Qui justificat impium, & qui condemnat justum, abominabilis est uterque apud Deum: & Isai. 5. Vae qui justificatis impium pro muneribus, & justitiam justi aufertis ab eo: & Luc. cap. 7. Justificata est sapientia ab omnibus filiis suis; & cap. 10. Ille autem volens justificare seipsum.
pass_a_gloss: Bellarmine teaches similar things in De Justif. book 1 chapter 3; among other things he observes that the name of justification in the sacred letters is taken for the acquisition of righteousness, as 1 Cor. 6. And such indeed you were, but you were washed, but you were sanctified, but you were justified. On Rom. 8: Whom he called, those he justified. Next, for the increase of righteousness. For, he says, just as in summer one is said to be warmed, not only who becomes hot from cold, but also who from hot becomes hotter; so also one is said to be justified, not only he who from impious becomes just, but also he who from just becomes more just. Thus Ecclesiasticus speaks, chapter 18: Do not fear to be justified unto death; and James in his Epistle, chapter 2: You see that a man is justified by works, and not by faith only; and John in the Apocalypse, chapter 22: He that is just, let him be justified still. Finally, for the declaration of righteousness, in a certain forensic mode, so that he is said to be justified who, when he was absent, or even guilty of some iniquity, is declared just by the judge through a sentence and is absolved. Thus Solomon uses this word, Proverbs 17; and Isaiah 5; and Luke 7 and 10.
pass_b_english: Bellarmine: justification = acquire righteousness, increase it, or forensically declare it.
Summer-heat analogy: not only cold→hot but hot→hotter = just→more just.
